analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal limits on toxic air pollution and sets rules to prevent catastrophic chemical accidents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in August 1989, sent to a subcommittee in October, and died there when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Air Act's program for hazardous air pollutants. It would have required the EPA to list many more toxic pollutants and set strict emission limits for industrial sources, with a 90% reduction set as the benchmark for existing sources. It also would have required plants that handle dangerous chemicals to assess their worst-case accident risks, created an independent Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board to investigate accidental releases, and funded monitoring of toxic air pollution in large urban areas. The bill was referred to committee and never received a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near industrial plants and in large urban areas, where hazardous air pollutants and the risk of sudden chemical releases are concentrated. The bill targeted urban monitoring grants at metropolitan areas over 250,000 people and required the worst-case release assessments to be made available to local emergency planners and, in most cases, the public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near industrial plants and cities

how_it_helps.text: It would have required the EPA to set emissions standards requiring the maximum achievable reduction in hazardous air pollutants, with a 90% reduction from uncontrolled levels written into the law as the benchmark for existing sources.

It would have required owners of facilities holding dangerous chemicals like chlorine, ammonia, and hydrofluoric acid to complete hazard assessments covering worst-case accidental releases, and to make those assessments available to local emergency planners and the public.

It would have created a Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board within the EPA to investigate accidental chemical releases and recommend prevention measures, with its findings generally open to the public.
It would have directed states with large metropolitan areas to monitor toxic pollutants in the ambient air and report the results and health risks to the public every two years.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical plants, refineries, coke ovens, and other industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants would bear the costs of emission controls, leak detection, monitoring, recordkeeping, and permit fees, and those costs could be passed on in product prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial plants that emit toxic air pollutants

drawbacks.text: For carcinogen and health-based standards, the bill barred the EPA from considering cost, cost-effectiveness, economic, energy, or technological feasibility in setting the level of protection, which critics of such rules argue can impose very high costs for small added health gains.

The bill imposed extensive new duties on industry — hazard assessments updated every two years, leak detection and monitoring, recordkeeping and reporting, and a permit program with fees — and allowed extensions of up to five additional years for existing sources facing extraordinary economic hardship, an acknowledgment of the compliance burden.
The bill authorized significant new spending, with appropriations authorized for fiscal years 1990 through 1994 and grants to states, costs borne by taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have imposed real and largely unavoidable costs on industrial emitters — the very costs that motivate opposition — in exchange for reduced exposure to toxic air pollutants and better protection against chemical accidents, with the largest benefits flowing to fenceline communities and big cities. Its ban on cost considerations for the strictest standards was its most aggressive feature and the easiest target for objection; the rest followed the structure that air-toxics reform eventually took.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in August 1989, moved to the Health and the Environment subcommittee in October, and died there when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991, never receiving a vote in committee or on the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Dennis Eckart introduced the Toxics Release Prevention Act on August 3, 1989, with two Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced.
On October 6, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; the record shows no further action, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and all bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial emitters of hazardous air pollutants — especially chemical manufacturers and refiners — were better off, because they avoided the emission limits, hazard assessments, permit fees, and Chemical Safety Board oversight the bill would have imposed. Communities near industrial facilities did not get the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial plants that emit toxic air pollutants

for.name: Rep. Dennis E. Eckart
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 3, 1989 and shepherded it as its sponsor.

for.name: 2 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only two cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill in August 1989 and never reported it out; the record shows no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only a Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors and no votes were ever taken, so no party split ever formed; its fate was decided by committee inaction rather than by a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected chemical facilities to strict hazardous-air-pollutant emission limits, two-year hazard assessments for dangerous substances, permit fees, and investigation of accidents by a new Chemical Safety Board. Because the bill died, the industry avoided these obligations during this Congress.

The bill directed the EPA to assess hazards from hydrogen sulfide released in oil and gas extraction and to develop a control strategy, a compliance cost for the industry, and the offsetting benefit of not passing would have kept those obligations off the books.

industries.industry: Air pollution control equipment and environmental monitoring firms
industries.note: Mandatory emission controls, leak detection systems, and urban air monitoring would have created demand for control technology and monitoring services. Because the bill never became law, this demand did not materialize from it.
